But in Hebr. Mashal always denotes representing discourse with the additional marks of the figurative and concise, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the section which presents (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Hab 2:6</reference>) him to whom it refers as a warning example, but particularly, as there defined, the gnome, the apothegm or maxim, in so far as this represents general truths in sharply outlined little pictures.
entries.5986face1f02c1e98c0d68bada9587a7d2ed5cd0: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference> <div eID="gen10539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10540" type="x-p"/> After the author has indicated the object which his Book of Proverbs is designed to subserve, and the fundamental principle on which it is based, he shows for whom he has intended it; he has particularly the rising generation in his eye: 8 Hear, my son, thy father’s instruction,    And refuse not the teaching of thy mother; 9 For these are a fair crown to thy head,    And Jewels to thy neck. “My son,” says the teacher of wisdom to the scholar whom he has, or imagines that he has, before him, addressing him as a fatherly friend. The N.T. representation of birth into a new spiritual life, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">1Co 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phlm.1.10">Phm 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Gal 4:19</reference>, lies outside the circle of the O.T. representation; the teacher feels himself as a father by virtue of his benevolent, guardian, tender love. Father and mother are the beloved parents of those who are addressed. When the Talmud understands אביך of God, אמּך of the people (אמּה), that is not the grammatico-historic meaning, but the practical interpretation and exposition, after the manner of the Midrash. The same admonition (with נצר, keep, instead of שׁמע, hear, and מצות, command, instead of מוּסר, instruction) is repeated in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.20">Pro 6:20</reference>, and what is said of the parents in one passage is in <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference> divided into two synonymous parallel passages. The stricter musar, which expresses the idea of sensible means of instruction (discipline), (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.24">Pro 13:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.15">Pro 22:15</reference>; Pro 23:13.), is suitably attributed to the father, and the torah to the mother, only administered by the word; Wisdom also always says תּורתי (my torah), and only once, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.10">Pro 8:10</reference>, מוּסרי (my musar).
entries.63933c34db5c2ccefdf4f407fce2bff751e96f44: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Pro 1:9</reference> הם, which is also used in the neut. <hi type="italic">illa</hi>, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.22.24">Job 22:24</reference>, refers here to the paternal discipline and the maternal teaching. These, obediently received and followed, are the fairest ornament of the child. לויה, from לוה, to wind, to roll, Arab. lawy (from לו, whence also לוּל = לולו, as דּוּד, to boil up, = דּודּו), means winding, twisted ornament, and especially wreath; a crown of gracefulness is equivalent to a graceful crown, a <hi type="italic">corolla gratiosa</hi>, as Schultens translates it; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.9">Pro 4:9</reference>, according to which, Wisdom bestows such a crown.<note placement="foot">In לוית חן the חן has the conjunctive accent <hi type="italic">shalsheleth</hi>, on account of which the <hi type="italic">Pesiq</hi> accent is omitted. This small <hi type="italic">shalsheleth</hi> occurs only eight times. See <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 36.</note> ענקים (or ענקות, Jdg 8:26) are necklaces, jewels for the neck; denom. of the Arab. 'unek, and Aram. עוּנק, the neck (perhaps from ענק = עוּק, to oppress, of heavy burdens; cf. αὐχήν, the neck). גּרגּות, is, like <hi type="italic">fauces</hi>, the throat by which one swallows (Arab. ǵarǵara, taǵarǵara), a plur. extensive (Böttcher, §695), and is better fitted than גּרון to indicate the external throat; Ezekiel, however, uses (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.11">Eze 16:11</reference>) garon, as our poet (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.22">Pro 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.21">Pro 6:21</reference>) uses garg'roth, to represent the front neck.<note placement="foot">The writing varies greatly. Here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.6.21">Pro 6:21</reference> we have לגרגּרתך; at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference>, על־גּרגּותך, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.22">Pro 3:22</reference>, לגרגּרתיך. Thus according to the Masora and correct texts.</note>
entries.6cb34eccb0a9777106da6479f5d25a360c4e1920: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.10">Pro 1:10</reference> <div eID="gen10540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10541" type="x-p"/> The general counsel of <reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Pro 1:9</reference> is here followed by a more special warning: <div eID="gen10541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10542" type="x-p"/> My son, if sinners entice thee <div eID="gen10542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10543" type="x-p"/> Consent thou not. <div eID="gen10543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10544" type="x-p"/> The בּני<note placement="foot">The accent <hi type="italic">Pazer</hi> over the בּני has the force of <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>.</note> (my son) is emphatically repeated. The intensive from חטּאים (signifies men to whom sin has become a habit, thus vicious, wicked. פּתּה (<hi type="italic">Pi</hi>. of פּתה, to open) is not denom., to make or wish to make a פּתי; the meaning, to entice (harmonizing with πείθειν), פּתּה obtains from the root-meaning of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, for it is related to it as <hi type="italic">pandere</hi> (<hi type="italic">januam</hi>) to <hi type="italic">patere</hi>: to open, to make accessible, susceptible, namely to persuasion. The warning 10b is as brief as possible a call of alarm back from the abyss. In the form תּבא (from אבה, to agree to, to be willing, see Wetstein in Job, p. 349) the preformative א is wanting, as in תּמרוּ, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sa 19:14</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">Psa 139:20</reference>, Ges. §68, 2, and instead of תּבה (= תּאבה, 1Ki 20:8) is vocalized not תּבא (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.25">Pro 11:25</reference>), but after the Aram. תּבא (cf. יגלי); see <reference osisRef="Gen.26.29">Gen 26:29</reference>, and <hi type="italic">Comment. on Isaiah</hi>, p. 648; Gesen. §75, 17. <div eID="gen10544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10545" type="x-p"/> Of the number of wicked men who gain associates to their palliation and strengthening, they are adduced as an example whom covetousness leads to murder. 11 If they say, “Go with us, we will lurk for blood,      Lie in wait for the innocent without cause; 12 Like the pit we will swallow them alive      And in perfect soundness like them that go down to the grave. 13 We find all manner of precious treasure,      Fill our houses with spoil. 14 Thou shalt cast thy lot amongst us,      We all have only one purse.”
entries.08aa9c18d9e00150ace89ee442c2f96699511c6c: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference> <div eID="gen10545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10546" type="x-p"/> The verb ארב signifies <hi type="italic">nectere</hi>, to bind fast (from רב, close, compact), (see under <reference osisRef="Isa.25.11">Isa 25:11</reference>), and particularly (but so that it bears in itself its object without ellipse) <hi type="italic">insidias nectere</hi> = <hi type="italic">insidiari</hi>. Regarding לדם Fleischer remarks: “Either elliptically for לשׁפּך־דּם (Jewish interp.), or, as the parallelism and the usage of the language of this book rather recommend, <hi type="italic">per synecd</hi>. for: for a man, with particular reference to his blood to be poured out (cf. our saying '<hi type="italic">ein junges Blut</hi>,' a young blood = a youth, with the underlying conception of the blood giving colour to the body as shining through it, or giving to it life and strength), as Psa 94:21.” As in post-biblical Heb. בּשׂר ודם (or inverted, αἱμα καὶ σάρξ, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb 2:14</reference>), used of men as such, is not so used in the O.T., yet דּם, like נפשׁ, is sometimes used synecdochically for the person, but never with reference to the blood as an essentially constituent part of corporealness, but always with reference to violent putting to death, which separates the blood from the body (cf. my <hi type="italic">System der bibl. Psychologie</hi>, p. 242). Here לדם is explained by לדמים, with which it is interchanged, Mic 7:2 : let us lurk for blood (to be poured out). The verb צפן is never, like טמן (to conceal), connected with חבלים, מוקשׁים ,ח, פּח, רשׁת - thus none of these words is here to be supplied; the idea of gaining over one expressed in the organic root צף (whence צפּה, <hi type="italic">diducendo obducere</hi>) has passed over into that of restraining oneself, watching, lurking, hence צפן (cog. Aram. כּמן) in the sense of <hi type="italic">speculari, insidiari</hi>, interchanges with צפה (to spy), (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">Psa 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32">Psa 37:32</reference>). The adv. חנּם (an old accus. from חן) properly means in a gracious manner, as a free gift (δωρεάν, <hi type="italic">gratis</hi> = <hi type="italic">gratiis</hi>), and accordingly, without reward, also without cause, which frequently = without guilt; but it never signifies <hi type="italic">sine effectu qui noceat</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, with impunity (Löwenst.). We have thus either to connect together נקי חנּם “innocent in vain” (as איבי חנּם, my enemies without a cause, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.52">Lam 3:52</reference>): his innocence helps him nothing whom God protects not against us notwithstanding his innocence (Schultens, Bertheau, Elster, and others); or connect חנם with the verb (lie in wait for), for which Hitzig, after the lxx, Syr., Rashi,<note placement="foot">Rashi, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, Rabbi Salomo Isaaki, of Troyes, died a.d. 1105. Ralbag, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, Rabbi Levi ben Gershon, usually referred to by Christian writers as Master Leo de Bannolis, or Gersonides, a native of Banolas near Gerona, died about 1342.</note> <div eID="gen10546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10547" type="x-p"/> Ralbag, Immanuel, rightly decides in view of <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.5">1Sa 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.31">1Sa 25:31</reference>; cf. also <reference osisRef="Job.9.17">Job 9:17</reference>, where the succession of the accents is the same (<hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> transmuted from <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>). Frequently there are combined together in his חנם (cf. Isa 28:14.), that which the author thinks, and that which those whom he introduces as speaking think.
entries.b576db6bb570bd59cf1801c5fc0be71563ffc0b9: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.12">Pro 1:12</reference> <div eID="gen10547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10548" type="x-p"/> The first clause of this verse Hitzig translates: “as the pit (swallows) that which lives.” This is untenable, because כּ with the force of a substantive (as <hi type="italic">instar</hi>, likeness) is regarded as a preposition, but not a conjunction (see at Psa 38:14.). חיּים (the living) is connected with נבלעם, and is the accus. of the state (hâl, according to the terminology of the Arab. grammarians) in which they will, with impunity, swallow them up like the pit (the insatiable, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pro 27:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.16">Pro 30:16</reference>), namely, while these their sacrifices are in the state of life’s freshness,<note placement="foot">Only in this sense is the existing accentuation of this verse (cf. the Targ.) to be justified.</note> “the living,” - without doubt, like <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.124.3">Psa 124:3</reference>, in fact and in expression an allusion to the fate of the company of Korah, Num 16:30, Num 16:33. If this is the meaning of חיים, then תּמימים as the parallel word means <hi type="italic">integros</hi> not in an ethical sense, in which it would be a synonym of נקי of <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Pro 29:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference>), but in a physical sense (<hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> καὶ τελείους; Parchon as Rashi, בריאים ושלמים, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Böttcher, De Inferis, §293). This physical sense is claimed for תּם, <reference osisRef="Job.21.23">Job 21:23</reference>, for תּם probably, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.4">Psa 73:4</reference>, and why should not תמים, used in the law regarding sacrifices (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.5">Exo 12:5</reference>, “without blemish”) of the faultlessness of the victim, also signify such an one אשׁר אין־בּו מתם (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa 1:6</reference>)? In the midst of complete external health they will devour them like those that go down to the grave (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.5">Psa 88:5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Isa 14:19</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, like those under whose feet the earth is suddenly opened, so that, without leaving any trace behind, they sink into the grave and into Hades. The connection of the finite with the accus. of place, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>, lies at the foundation of the genitive connection יורדי בור (with the tone thrown back): those that go down to the grave.
entries.b6de12748ef456f47f8221996cc815f802b20c94: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.13-Prov.1.14">Pro 1:13-14</reference><note placement="foot">Here, in <reference osisRef="Prov.1.14">Pro 1:14</reference>, גורלך is to be written with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> (not <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>) in the second syllable; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 20. <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, vii. §2.</note> <div eID="gen10548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10549" type="x-p"/> To their invitation, bearing in itself its own condemnation, they add as a lure the splendid self-enriching treasures which in equal and just fellowship with them they may have the prospect of sharing. הון (from הוּן, <hi type="italic">levem</hi>, then <hi type="italic">facilem esse</hi>, <hi type="italic">être aisé, à son aise</hi>) means <hi type="italic">aisance</hi>, convenience, opulence, and concretely that by which life is made agreeable, thus money and possessions (Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterbuch</hi>, i. 423f.). With this הון with remarkable frequency in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> יקר (from יקר, Arab. waḳar, <hi type="italic">grave esse</hi>) is connected in direct contrast, according to its primary signification; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Pro 12:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.4">Pro 24:4</reference> : heavy treasures which make life light. Yet it must not be maintained that, as Schultens has remarked, this oxymoron is intended, nor also that it is only consciously present in the language. מצא has here its primitive appropriate signification of attaining, as <reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">Isa 10:14</reference> of reaching. שׁלל (from שׁלל, to draw from, draw out, from של, cf. שׁלה, שׁלף, Arab. salab, <hi type="italic">Comm. on Isa.</hi> p. 447) is that which is drawn away from the enemy, <hi type="italic">exuviae</hi>, and then the booty and spoil taken in war generally. נמלּא, to fill with anything, make full, governs a double accusative, as the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> (to become full of anything) governs only one. In <reference osisRef="Prov.1.14">Pro 1:14</reference>, the invitation shows how the prospect is to be realized. Interpreters have difficulty in conceiving what is here meant. Do not a share by lot and a common purse exclude one another? Will they truly, in the distribution of the booty by lot, have equal portions at length, equally much in their money-bags? Or is it meant that, apart from the portion of the booty which falls to every one by lot, they have a common purse which, when their business is ebbing, must supply the wants of the company, and on which the new companion can maintain himself beforehand? Or does it mean only that they will be as mutually helpful to one another, according to the principle τὰ τῶν φίλων κοινά (<hi type="italic">amicorum omnia communia</hi>), as if they had only one purse? The meaning is perfectly simple. The oneness of the purse consists in this, that the booty which each of them gets, belongs not wholly or chiefly to him, but to the whole together, and is disposed of by lot; so that, as far as possible, he who participated not at all in the affair in obtaining it, may yet draw the greatest prize. This view harmonizes the relation between 14b and 14a. The common Semitic כּים is even used at the present day in Syria and elsewhere as the name of the Exchange (“<hi type="italic">Börse</hi>”) (plur. akjâs); here it is the purse (“<hi type="italic">Kasse</hi>”) (χρημάτων δοχεῖον, Procop.), which is made up of the profits of the business. This profit consists not merely in gold, but is here thought of in regard to its worth in gold. The apparent contradiction between distributing by lot and having a common purse disappears when the distribution by lot of the common property is so made, that the retaining of a stock-capital, or reserve fund, is not excluded.
entries.b6b78d01fa66b40e45974d3f4deb761d9c1ad0c0: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.15">Pro 1:15</reference> <div eID="gen10549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10550" type="x-p"/> After the men are described against whose enticements a warning is given forth, the warning is emphatically repeated, and is confirmed by a threefold reason: <div eID="gen10550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10551" type="x-p"/> My son! go not in the way with them. <div eID="gen10551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10552" type="x-p"/> Keep back thy foot from their path. <div eID="gen10552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10553" type="x-p"/> If בּדרך (in the way), taken alone, cannot be equivalent to בדרך אחד (in one way), so is אתּם (with them) to be regarded as its determination.<note placement="foot">The Arab. grammarians regard this as half determination, and call it takhsys; that אתּם has with them the force of a virtually coordinated attributive; while, according to the Arab. gram., it is also possible that בּדרך, “in one way,” is equivalent to on the common way, for in the indetermination sometimes there lies the conception not merely of âhad, but of weahad.</note> <div eID="gen10553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10554" type="x-p"/> Foot (not feet), as eye, hand, etc., is used where the members come less under consideration than what they unitedly bring about (Pro 4:26.). נתיבה, from נתב, signifies properly that which is raised, especially the (raised) footstep.
entries.c82e385b81765bf3c9a63ca15b6d32ae9cdf3f6b: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference> <div eID="gen10554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">first</hi> argument to enforce the warning: <div eID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10556" type="x-p"/> For their feet run to the evil, <div eID="gen10556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> And hasten to shed blood. <div eID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> That this is their object they make no secret (Pro 1:11.); but why is it that such an object as this should furnish no ground of warning against them, especially as on this beginning the stamp of that which is morally blamable is here impressed with לרע? Besides, this circular movement of the thoughts is quite after the manner of this poet; and that <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference> is his style, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.18">Pro 6:18</reference> shows. The want of this distich (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference> = <reference osisRef="Rom.3.15">Rom 3:15</reference>) in lxx B. א. weighs heavier certainly than the presence of it in lxx A. (Procop., Syro-Hezap.), since the translation is not independent, but is transferred from <reference osisRef="Isa.59.7">Isa 59:7</reference>; but if for the first time, at a later period, it is supplied in the lxx, yet it has the appearance of an addition made to the Hebr. text from <reference osisRef="Isa.59.7">Isa 59:7</reference> (Hitzig, Lagarde); cf. <hi type="italic">Comm. on Isaiah</hi>, 40-66. לשׁפּך is always pointed thus; for, as a regular rule, after ל as well as מ sa llew s the aspiration disappears; but in <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.17">Eze 17:17</reference> בּשׁפּך is also found, and in this case (cf. at <reference osisRef="Ps.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference>) the punctuation is thus inconsequent.
entries.4e373c01c4315e31567a08c4e182834b720ebd61: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Pro 1:17</reference> <div eID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10559" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">second</hi> argument in support of the warning. <div eID="gen10559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> For in vain is the net spread out <div eID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> In the eyes of all (the winged) birds. <div eID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10562" type="x-p"/> The interpretation <hi type="italic">conspersum est rete</hi>, namely, with corn as a bait, which was put into circulation by Rashi, is inadmissible; for as little as הזּה (<hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of נזה) can mean to strew, can זרה mean to spread. The object is always that which is scattered (<hi type="italic">gestreut</hi>), not that which is spread (<hi type="italic">bestreut</hi>). Thus, <hi type="italic">expansum est rete</hi>, but not from מזר, <hi type="italic">extendere</hi>, from which מזורה<note placement="foot">The MS Masora remarks לית וחסר, and hence מזרה is written defectively in the Erfurt, 1, 2, 3, Frankf. 1294, in the edition of Norzi and elsewhere.</note> in this form cannot be derived (it would in that case be מזוּרה), but from זרה, pass. of זרה, to scatter, spread out. The alluring net, when it is shaken out and spread, is, as it were, scattered, <hi type="italic">ventilatur</hi>. But if this is done incautiously before the eyes of the birds to be caught, they forthwith fly away. The principle stress lies on the בּעיני (before the eyes) as the reason of the חנּם (in vain), according to the saying of Ovid, <hi type="italic">Quae nimis apparent retia, vitat avis</hi>. The <hi type="italic">applicatio similitudinis</hi> lying near, according to J. H. Michaelis, is missed even by himself and by most others. If the poet wished to say that they carried on their work of blood with such open boldness, that he must be more than a simpleton who would allow himself to be caught by them, that would be an unsuitable ground of warning; for would there not be equally great need for warning against fellowship with them, if they had begun their enticement with more cunning, and reckoned on greater success? Hitzig, Ewald, Zöckler, and others, therefore interpret חנם, not in the sense of in vain, inasmuch as they do not let themselves be caught; but: in vain, for they see not the net, but only the scattered corn. But according to the preceding, הרשׁת (the net) leads us to think only either of the net of the malicious designs, or the net of the alluring deceptions. Thus, as Ziegler has noticed, the warned ought to make application of the similitude to himself: Go not with them, for their intention is bad; go not with them, for if the bird flees away from the net which is spread out before it, thou wilt not surely be so blind as suffer thyself to be ensnared by their gross enticements. בּעל כּנף: the furnished with the wing (wings in <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">Ecc 10:20</reference>); בּעל forms the idea of property (lord).
entries.ccc5051d0960b4ac0665dd6e728166639fbc921f: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.18">Pro 1:18</reference> <div eID="gen10562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10563" type="x-p"/> The causal conj. כּי (for) in <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Pro 1:17</reference> are coordinated; and there now follows, introduced by the conj. ו (“and”), a <hi type="italic">third</hi> reason for the warning: <div eID="gen10563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> And they lie in wait for their own blood, <div eID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10565" type="x-p"/> They lay snares for their own lives. <div eID="gen10565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> The warning of <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference> is founded on the immorality of the conduct of the enticer; that of <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Pro 1:17</reference> on the audaciousness of the seduction as such, and now on the self-destruction which the robber and murderer bring upon themselves: they wish to murder others, but, as the result shows, they only murder themselves. The expression is shaped after <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference>, as if it were: They lay snares, as they themselves say, for the blood of others; but it is in reality for their own blood: they certainly lie in wait, as they say; but not, as they add, for the innocent, but for their own lives (Fl.). Instead of לדמם, there might be used לדמיהם, after Mic 7:2; but לנפשׁם would signify <hi type="italic">ipsis</hi> (post-biblical, לעצמם), while לנפשׁתם leaves unobliterated the idea of the life: <hi type="italic">animis ipsorum</hi>; for if the O.T. language seeks to express <hi type="italic">ipse</hi> in any other way than by the personal pronoun spoken emphatically, this is done by the addition of נפשׁ (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa 53:11</reference>). המו was on this account necessary, because <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Pro 1:17</reference> has another subject (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>).
entries.72c8cae32baeb3eab27a0d6badcefd9015752dc5: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.19">Pro 1:19</reference> <div eID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> An <hi type="italic">epiphonema</hi>: <div eID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10568" type="x-p"/> Such is the lot of all who indulge in covetousness; <div eID="gen10568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10569" type="x-p"/> It takes away the life of its owner. <div eID="gen10569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10570" type="x-p"/> This language is formed after Job 8:13. Here, as there, in the word ארחות, the ideas of action and issue, manner of life and its result, are all combined. בּצע signifies properly that which is cut off, a piece, fragment broken off, then that which one breaks off and takes to himself - booty, gain, particularly unjust gain (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.16">Pro 28:16</reference>). בּצע בּצע is he who is greedy or covetous. The subject to יקּח is בּצע, covetousness, πλεονεξία (see <reference osisRef="Isa.57.17">Isa 57:17</reference>). As Hoses, <reference osisRef="Job.4.11">Job 4:11</reference>, says of three other things that they taken away לב, the understanding (νοῦς), so here we are taught regarding unjust gain or covetousness, that it takes away נפשׁ, the life (ψυχή) (לקח נפשׁ, to take away the life, 1Ki 19:10; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.14">Psa 31:14</reference>). בּעליו denotes not the possessor of unjust gain, but as an inward conception, like בעל אף, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.24">Pro 22:24</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.2">Pro 23:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.8">Pro 24:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.11">Ecc 10:11</reference>, him of whom covetousness is the property. The sing. נפשׁ does not show that בּעליו is thought of as sing.; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.23">Pro 22:23</reference>, Ps. 34:23; but according to <reference osisRef="Prov.3.27">Pro 3:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.22">Pro 16:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Ecc 8:8</reference>, this is nevertheless probable, although the usage without the suffix is always בּעל בּצע, and not בּעלי (of plur. intens. בּעלים).
entries.b55728884bbf4c978d96c43212845ed8a96cf49d: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference> <div eID="gen10570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10571" type="x-p"/> Looking to its form and vocalization, חכמות may be an Aramaizing abstract formation (Gesen.; Ew. 165, <hi type="italic">c</hi>; Olsh. 219, <hi type="italic">b</hi>); for although the forms אחות and גּלות are of a different origin, yet in רבּות and הוללות such abstract formations lie before us. The termination ûth is here, by the passing over of the <hi type="italic">u</hi> into the less obscure but more intensive <hi type="italic">o</hi> (cf. יהו in the beginning and middle of the word, and יהוּ יהו at the end of the word), raised to ôth, and thereby is brought near to the fem. plur. (cf. חכמות, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.1">Pro 14:1</reference>, <hi type="italic">sapientia</hi>, as our plur. of the neut. <hi type="italic">sapiens</hi>, חכמה), approaching to the abstract. On the other hand, that חכמות is sing. of abstract signification, is not decisively denoted by its being joined to the plur. of the predicate (for תּרנּה here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">Pro 8:3</reference>, is scarcely plur.; and if ראמות, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.7">Pro 24:7</reference>, is plur., חכמות as the numerical plur. may refer to the different sciences or departments of knowledge); but perhaps by this, that it interchanges with תּבוּנות, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.4">Psa 49:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.12">Pro 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.16">Pro 28:16</reference>, and that an abstract formation from חכמה (fem. of חכם, חכם), which besides is not concrete, was unnecessary. Still less is חכמות = חכמת a singular, which has it in view to change חכמה into a proper name, for proof of which Hitzig refers to תּהומות, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.15">Psa 78:15</reference>; the singular ending ôth without an abstract signification does not exist. After that Dietrich, in his <hi type="italic">Abhandl</hi>. 1846, has shown that the origin of the plur. proceeds not from separate calculation, but from comprehension,<note placement="foot">In the Indo-Germanic languages the <hi type="italic">s</hi> of the plur. also probably proceeds from the prep. <hi type="italic">sa</hi> (<hi type="italic">sam</hi>) = συν. See Schleicher, <hi type="italic">Compend. der vergl. Gram.</hi> §247.</note> and that particularly also names denoting intellectual strength are frequently plur., which multiply the conception not externally but internally, there is no longer any justifiable doubt that חכמות signifies the all-comprehending, absolute, or, as Böttcher, §689, expresses it, the full personal wisdom. Since such intensive plurals are sometimes united with the plur. of the predicate, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the monotheistically interpreted Elohim, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">Gen 35:7</reference> (see l.c.), so תּרנּה may be plur. On the other hand, the idea that it is a <hi type="italic">forma mixta</hi> of תּרן (from רנן) and תּרנה (<reference osisRef="Job.39.23">Job 39:23</reference>) or תּרנּה, the final sound in <hi type="italic">ah</hi> opposes. It may, however, be the emphatic form of the 3rd fem. sing. of רנן; for, that the Hebr. has such an emphatic form, corresponding to the Arab. taktubanna, is shown by these three examples (keeping out of view the suspicion of a corruption of the text, Olsh. p. 452), Jdg 5:26; <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.3">Isa 28:3</reference>; cf. תּשׁלחנה, Oba 1:13 (see Caspari, l.c.), an example of the 2nd masc. sing. of this formation. רנן (with רנה) is a word imitative of sound (Schallwort), used to denote “a clear-sounding, shrill voice (thence the Arab. rannan, of a speaker who has a clear, piercing voice); then the clear shrill sound of a string or chord of a bow, or the clear tinkle of the arrow in the quiver, and of the metal that has been struck” (Fl.). The meaning of רחבות is covered by <hi type="italic">plateae</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.21">Luk 14:21</reference>), wide places; and חוּץ, which elsewhere may mean that which is without, before the gates of the city and courts, here means the “open air,” in contradistinction to the inside of the houses.
entries.6b25c03e375cd5fd902dad1d42c7e531b324fdad: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Pro 1:21</reference> המיּות (plur. of הומי, the ground-form of הומה, from המי = המה), “they who are making noise;” for the epithet is poetically used (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>) as a substantive, crowded noisy streets or places. ראשׁ is the place from which on several sides streets go forth: cf. ras el-ain, the place where the well breaks forth; ras en-nahr, the place from which the stream divides itself; the sing. is meant distributively as little as at Pro 8:2. פּתח, if distinguished from שׁער (which also signifies cleft, breach), is the opening of the gate, the entrance by the gate. Four times the poet says that Wisdom goes forth preaching, and four times that she preaches publicly; the בּעיר used in five places implies that Wisdom preaches not in the field, before the few who there are met with, but in the city, which is full of people.
entries.7bca9bce27b8f528ba5a718c76461fe25e922ad2: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.22">Pro 1:22</reference> <div eID="gen10571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10572" type="x-p"/> The poet has now reached that part of his introduction where he makes use of the very words uttered by Wisdom: <div eID="gen10572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10573" type="x-p"/> How long, ye simple, will ye love simplicity, <div eID="gen10573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10574" type="x-p"/> And scorners delight in scorning, <div eID="gen10574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10575" type="x-p"/> And fools hate knowledge? <div eID="gen10575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10576" type="x-p"/> Three classes of men are here addressed: the פּתים, the simple, who, being accessible to seduction, are only too susceptible of evil; the לצים, mockers, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, free-thinkers (from לוּץ, Arab. luṣ, <hi type="italic">flectere, torquere</hi>, properly <hi type="italic">qui verbis obliquis utitur</hi>); and the כּסילים, fools, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the mentally imbecile and stupid (from כּסל, Arab. kasal, to be thick, coarse, indolent). The address to these passes immediately over into a declaration regarding them; cf. the same enallage, Pro 1:27. עד־מתי has the accent <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>, on account of the <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> following; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 26. Intentionally, Wisdom addresses only the פתים, to whom she expects to find soonest access. Between the futt., which express the continuing love and hatred, stands the perf. חמדוּ, which expresses that in which the mockers found pleasure, that which was the object of their love. להם is the so-called <hi type="italic">dat. ethicus</hi>, which reflexively refers to that which is said to be the will and pleasure of the subject; as we say, “I am fond of this and that.” The form תּאהבוּ, Abulwalîd, Parchon, and Kimchi regard as <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>; but תּאהבוּ instead of תּאהבוּ would be a <hi type="italic">recompensatio</hi> of the virtual doubling, defacing the character of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>. Schultens regards it as a defectively written <hi type="italic">Paiël</hi> (in Syr.), but it is not proved that this conjugation exists in Hebr.; much rather תּאהבוּ is the only possible <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> form with תּאהבוּן without the pause, regularly formed from תּאהבוּ (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ewald, §193, a). The division by the accent <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>-<hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> of the two words תאהבו פתי is equal in value to the connecting of them by <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi>, p. x. In codd., and also in correct texts, תאהבו is written with the accent <hi type="italic">Galgal</hi> on the first syllable, as the servant of the <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>-<hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> is incorrectly here and there placed under the תּ.
entries.c101e86fe0621ea154dff60a58e1a8ac1065e819: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.23">Pro 1:23</reference> <div eID="gen10576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10577" type="x-p"/> To the call to thoughtfulness which lies in the complaint “How long?” there follows the entreaty: <div eID="gen10577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10578" type="x-p"/> Turn ye at my reproof! <div eID="gen10578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10579" type="x-p"/> Behold! I would pour out my Spirit upon you, <div eID="gen10579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10580" type="x-p"/> I would make you to know my words. 23a is not a clause expressive of a wish, which with the particle expressive of a wish, which is wanting, would be תּשׁוּבוּ־נא, or according to <reference osisRef="Prov.23.1">Pro 23:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Pro 27:23</reference> would be שׁוב תּשׁוּבוּ. The הנּה, introducing the principal clause, stamps 23a as the conditional clause; the relation of the expressions is as <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Isa 26:10</reference>; Job 20:24. תּשׁוּבוּ<note placement="foot">In the <hi type="italic">Hagiographa</hi> everywhere written <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, with exception of Job 17:10.</note> is not equivalent to <hi type="italic">si convertamini</hi>, which would require תּפנוּ, but to <hi type="italic">si revertamini</hi>; but לתוכהתּי<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> belongs to the ת, under which it should be placed (and not to the ל), as the commencing sound of the second syllable before the tone-syllable; cf. Pro 1:25.</note> does not therefore mean at my reproof, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in consequence of it (Hitzig, after Num 16:34), but it is a <hi type="italic">constructio praegnans</hi>: turning and placing yourselves under my reproof. With תוכחת there is supposed an ἔλεγχος (lxx, Symm.): bringing proof, conviction, punishment. If they, leaving their hitherto accustomed way, permit themselves to be warned against their wickedness, then would Wisdom cause her words to flow forth to them, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, would without reserve disclose and communicate to them her spirit, cause them to know (namely by experience) her words. הבּיע (from נבע, R. נב; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Genesis, p. 635) is a common figurative word, expressive of the free pouring forth of thoughts and words, for the mouth is conceived of as a fountain (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">Pro 18:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="Matt.12.34">Mat 12:34</reference>), and the ῥῆσις (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., lxx) as ῥεῦσις; only here it has the Spirit as object, but parallel with דּברי, thus the Spirit as the active power of the words, which, if the Spirit expresses Himself in them, are πνεῦμα καὶ ζωή, Joh 6:63. The addresses of Wisdom in the Book of Proverbs touch closely upon the discourses of the Lord in the Logos-Gospel. Wisdom appears here as the fountain of the words of salvation for men; and these words of salvation are related to her, just as the λόγοι to the divine λόγος expressing Himself therein.
entries.106b92d053db448a46f9451a60d19ddb567fec86: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24-Prov.1.27">Pro 1:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen10580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10581" type="x-p"/> The address of Wisdom now takes another course. Between <reference osisRef="Prov.1.23">Pro 1:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">Pro 1:24</reference> there is a pause, as between <reference osisRef="Isa.1.20">Isa 1:20</reference> and Isa 1:21. In vain Wisdom expects that her complaints and enticements will be heard. Therefore she turns her call to repentance into a discourse announcing judgment. 24 Because I have called, and ye refused;      Stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; 25 And ye have rejected all my counsel      And to my reproof have not yielded: 26 Therefore will I also laugh at your calamity,      Will mock when your terror cometh; 27 When like a storm your terror cometh,      And your destruction swept on like a whirlwind;      When distress and anguish cometh upon you. <div eID="gen10581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10582" type="x-p"/> Commencing with יען (which, like מען, from ענה, to oppose, denotes the intention, but more the fundamental reason or the cause than, as למען, the motive or object), the clause, connected with גּם־אני, <hi type="italic">ego vicissim</hi>, turns to the conclusion. As here יען קראתי (as the word of Jahve) are connected by גּם־אני to the expression of the <hi type="italic">talio</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa 66:4</reference>, so also מאם, with its contrast אבה, Isa 1:19. The construction <hi type="italic">quoniam vocavi et renuistis for quoniam quum vocarem renuistis</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa 12:1</reference>) is the common diffuse (<hi type="italic">zerstreute</hi>) Semitic, the paratactic instead of the periodizing style. The stretching out of the hand is, like the “spreading out” in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.2">Isa 65:2</reference>, significant of striving to beckon to the wandering, and to bring them near. Regarding הקשׁיב, viz., אזנו, to make the ear still (R. קש), <hi type="italic">arrigere</hi>, incorrectly explained by Schultens, after the Arab ḳashab, <hi type="italic">polire</hi>, by <hi type="italic">aurem purgare</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Isaiah, p. 257, note.
entries.e0304a6f1090d38954aea7433847971c90718492: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28-Prov.1.31">Pro 1:28-31</reference> <div eID="gen10582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10583" type="x-p"/> Then - this sublime preacher in the streets continues - distress shall teach them to pray: 28 Then shall they call on me, and I will not answer;      They shall early seek after me, and not find me; 29 Because that they hated knowledge,      And did not choose the fear of Jahve. 30 They have not yielded to my counsel,      Despised all my reproof: 31 Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their way,      And satiate themselves with their own counsels. <div eID="gen10583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10584" type="x-p"/> In the full emphatic forms, יקראנני, they shall call on me, ישׁחרנני, they shall seek me, and ימצאנני, they shall find me, the suffix ני may be joined to the old plur. ending ûn (Gesenius, Olshausen, Böttcher); but open forms like יברכנהוּ, He will bless him,יכבּדנני, He will honour me (from יכבּדנּי), and the like, rather favour the conclusion that נ is epenthetic (Ew. §250, b).<note placement="foot">In the Codd. יקראנני is written; in this case the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> indicates the tone syllable: <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 7 note, p. 21 note; and <hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, ii. §1, note. In ישׁחרנני the <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> is to be placed over the ר. In the <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>-word ימצאנני it appears undoubtedly that the form is to be spoken as <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, with tone on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen10584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10585" type="x-p"/> The address here takes the form of a declaration: <hi type="italic">Stultos nunc indignos censet ulteriori alloquio</hi> (Mich.). It is that laughter and scorn, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.26">Pro 1:26</reference>, which here sounds forth from the address of the Judge regarding the incorrigible. שׁחר is denom. of שׁחר, to go out and to seek with the morning twilight, as also בּקּר, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>, perhaps to appear early, and usually (Arab.) bakar (I, II, IV), to rise early, to be zealous (Lane: “He hastened to do or accomplish, or attain the thing needed”). Zöckler, with Hitzig, erroneously regards <reference osisRef="Prov.1.29">Pro 1:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.30">Pro 1:30</reference> as the antecedent to Pro 1:31. With ויאכלוּ, “and they shall eat,” the futt. announcing judgment are continued from <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Pro 1:28</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.46">Deu 28:46</reference>-48. The conclusion after תּהת כּי, “therefore because,” or as usually expressed (except here and <reference osisRef="Deut.4.37">Deu 4:37</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.4.25">Gen 4:25</reference>), תּהת אשׁר (ἀνθ ̓ ὧν), is otherwise characterized, <reference osisRef="Deut.22.29">Deu 22:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.12">2Ch 21:12</reference>; and besides, תהת אשׁר stands after (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.21">1Sa 26:21</reference>; 2Ki 22:17; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.19">Jer 29:19</reference>) oftener than before the principal clause. בּחר combines in itself the meanings of <hi type="italic">eligere</hi> and <hi type="italic">diligere</hi> (Fl.). The construction of אבה ל (to be inclining towards) follows that of the analogous שׁמע ל (to hear). Each one eats of the fruit of his way - good fruit of good ways (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Isa 3:10</reference>), and evil fruit of evil ways. “The מן, 31b, introduces the object from which, as a whole, that which one eats, and with which he is satisfied, is taken as a part, or the object from which, as from a fountain, satisfaction flows forth” (Fl.). In correct texts, ויאכלוּ has the accent <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, and at the same time <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> as its servant. Regarding the laws of punctuation, according to which וּממּעצתיהם (with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> on the tone-syllable, <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> on the antepenult, and <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> before the <hi type="italic">Chateph-Pathach</hi>) is to be written, see Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 11, <hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, iv. §4. Norzi accents the word incorrectly with <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>. With the exception of <reference osisRef="Prov.22.22">Pro 22:22</reference>, the pluralet<note placement="foot">A plur. denoting unity in the circumstances, and a similarity in the relations of time and space.</note> מועצות has always the meaning of ungodly counsels.
entries.37a7148c77eff6a49af5582ede32548e48536a51: <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32-Prov.1.33">Pro 1:32-33</reference> <div eID="gen10585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10586" type="x-p"/> The discourse is now summarily brought to a close: 32 For the perverseness of the simple slays them,      And the security of fools destroys them. 33 But whoever harkeneth to me dwells secure,      And is at rest from fear of evil. <div eID="gen10586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10587" type="x-p"/> Of the two interpretations of שׁוּב, a turning towards (with אל and the like, conversion) or a turning away (with מאחרי or מעל, desertion), in משׁוּבה the latter (as in the post-Bib. תּשׁוּבה, repentance, the former) is expressed; apostasy from wisdom and from God are conjoined. שׁלוה is here <hi type="italic">carnalis securitas</hi>; but the word may also denote the external and the internal peace of the righteous, as שׁאנן, whence שׁלאנן, <reference osisRef="Job.21.23">Job 21:23</reference>, as a superlative is formed by the insertion of the ל of שׁלו, is taken <hi type="italic">in bonam et malam partem</hi>. שׁאנן is, according to the Masora (also in <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">Jer 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.27">Jer 46:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jer 48:11</reference>), 3rd perf. Pilel (Ewald, §120, a), from the unused שׁאן, to be quiet: he has attained to full quietness, and enjoys such. The construction with מן follows the analogy of הניח מן (to give rest from), שׁקט מן (to rest from), and the like. The negative interpretation of מן, <hi type="italic">sine ullo pavore mali</hi> (Schultens, Ewald), is unnecessary; also <reference osisRef="Job.21.9">Job 21:9</reference> may be explained by “peace from terror,” especially since שׁלום is derived from the root של, <hi type="italic">extrahere</hi>. פּחד רעה, “fear of evil,” one may perhaps distinguish from פחד רע as the genitive of combination.  <chapter eID="Prov.1"/> <div eID="gen10587" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THe <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap>in 4. 32. Chap. 10. 1. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 1.</ns0:note> proverbs <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Proverbs are ancient, and wise, and short Sayings in common use: whereof some are plain and easie, others are intricate and obscure.</ns0:note> of Solomon <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Proceeding from <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> and most of them digested by him into this Book. See the Preface.</ns0:note>, the son of David, king of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. To know <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Written to help men to know throughly and practically.</ns0:note> wisdom <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Both humane Wisdom to conduct our Affairs in this Life, which divers of the following Proverbs do, and especially divine Wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom which <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> chiefly designed, or to make men wise to know their duty, and to save their Souls.</ns0:note> and instruction <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Counsels and Instructi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons delivered either by God, or by Men, in order to the attainment of Wisdom.</ns0:note>, to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive the words of understanding <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. Which are the effects of a good under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing: Or 2. Which teach a man true Understanding, whereby to discern between Truth and Error, between Good and Evil, to chuse the former, and to refuse the latter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. To receive the instruction <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Willingly to receive the Counsels of others, which is a good step to Wisdom, and a part of it.</ns0:note> of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> wisdom <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Such as is wise, and tends to make men wise and prudent. This is opposed to <ns0:hi>the Instruction of Fools</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>folly,</ns0:hi> of which <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 16. 22 & 19. 27. For folly or wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />edness hath its School, and multitudes of Scholars, that are very apt to learn its Lessons.</ns0:note>, ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stice, and judgment, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> equity <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which teach men just judgment or equity, to wit, their whole Duty, both to God and to others, and to themselves. These three words seem to signifie the same thing, and are heaped together to note either the necessity of the Precept, or the exactness and diligence which is required in the practice of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. To give subtilty <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>Prudence,</ns0:hi> as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3. 21. & 5. 2. & 8. 5, 12. which elsewhere is taken in an evil sense for <ns0:hi>craft</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>subtilty.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> to the simple <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Such as want wisdom, and are easily deceived by others, and therefore most need this blessing.</ns0:note>, to the young man <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which wants both Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perience and Self-government.</ns0:note> knowledge and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>advise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> discretion.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9. 9.</ns0:note> A wise <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> will hear <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Is not self-conceited, as Fools are, but willing to learn from others; and therefore will attend to the following Instructions.</ns0:note>, and will encrease learning <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And thereby will gain this great benefit to grow in knowledge and wisdom. This he adds to shew that this Book is useful and necessa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, not only to the simple, but also to the most wise and knowing Persons.</ns0:note>: and a man of understanding shall attain un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to wise counsels <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Not to deep speculations, but practical consideration, to the art of governing himself or others well and prudently.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. To understand a proverb and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>an elo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> speech.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the interpreta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Interpretation of a Proverb, by a Figure called <ns0:hi>Hen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diaduo,</ns0:hi> or the meaning and use of the wise sayings of God, or of men; to know this practically, and for his direction and benefit; for practice is the great design of this Book.</ns0:note>; the words of the wise, and their dark say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Such as are hard to be understood by inconsiderate and ungodly men, but to be found out by diligent and humble enquiry.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 28. 28. Psal. 111. 10. Chap. 9. 10. Eccl. 12. 13.</ns0:note> The fear of the LORD <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Reverence and obedience to God, or his Worship and Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice, as this word is commonly used.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> the prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cipal part.</ns0:note> the beginning <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either the Foundation, or the Top, and Perfection, or chief Point, without which all other knowledge is vain and useless.</ns0:note> of knowledge: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> fools <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Wicked men, called <ns0:hi>Fools</ns0:hi> through this whole Book, such as do not fear God.</ns0:note> despise wisdom and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Are so far from at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />taining true Wisdom, that they despise it, and all the means of getting it. Which fully proves what he now said, that <ns0:hi>the Fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. My son <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">He speaks to his Scholars with paternal Authority and Affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to make them more attentive and obedient. Teachers among the Hebrews and others, were commonly called <ns0:hi>Fathers,</ns0:hi> and their Scholars their <ns0:hi>Sons.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6. 20.</ns0:note> hear the instruction of thy father <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">His good and wholsome Counsels, but not such as are contrary to Gods Law, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 19. 27.</ns0:note>, and forsake not the law of thy mother <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Those pious instructions which thy Mother instilled into thee in thy tender years. See <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 31. 1. 2 <ns0:hi>T<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>m.</ns0:hi> 1. 5. & 3. 14, 15. This he adds, because Children when grown up, are very prone to sleight their Mothers advice, because of the infirmity of their Sex, and because they have not that dependence upon, and Expectation from their Mothers which they have from their Fathers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. For they <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> an ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding.</ns0:note> an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This will make thee amiable and honourable in the fight of God and of men, whereas the forsaking of those good Counsels will make thee contemptible.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. My son, if sinners <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Eminently so called, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13. 13, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 1. 1. & 26. 9. such as sell themselves to work all manner of Wickedness, particularly Thieves, and Robbers, and Murtherers, as appears from the next verses, as also Oppressors and Cheaters, by comparing this with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note> entice thee, consent thou not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. If they say, come with us <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">We are numerous, and strong, and sociable.</ns0:note>, let us lay wait for blood <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To shed Blood. He expresseth not their words, which would rather af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fright than inveigle a young novice, but the true nature and conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quence of the Action, and what lies at the bottom of their speci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous pretences.</ns0:note>, let us lurk privily <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">So we shall neither be prevented before, nor discovered and punished afterward.</ns0:note> for the innocent <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Harmless Travellers, who are more careless and secure, and unprovided for opposition, than such Villains as themselves.</ns0:note> with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out cause <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Though they have not provoked us, nor deserved this usage from us.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>h</ns0:hi> This <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> adds to discover their malignity and baseness, and so deter the young Man from association with them.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. Let us swallow them up alive as <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>hell.</ns0:hi> Num. 16. 33.</ns0:note> the grave <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which speedily covers and consumes dead Bodies. See <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 55. 15. & 124. 3. We shall do our work quickly, easily, and with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out fear of discovery.</ns0:note>, and whole, as those that go down into the pit <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">into some deep Pit, into which a Tra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veller falls unawares, and is utterly lost and never discovered.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoil <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">As our danger is little, so our profit will be great.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:518" />14 Cast in thy lot among us <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Put in thy Money into our Stock. Or rather, <ns0:hi>thou shalt cast thy lot amongst us,</ns0:hi> i. e. thou shalt have a share with us, and that equally and by lot, although thou art but a Novice and we Veteranes. This agrees best with their design, which was to allure him by the promise of advantage.</ns0:note>, let us all have one purse <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or. <ns0:hi>we will have,</ns0:hi> &c. One Purse shall re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive all our profits and furnish us with all expences. So we shall live with great facility and true friendship.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. My Son <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 4. 14.</ns0:note>, walk not thou in the way with them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Avoid their courses, and their conversation, and company.</ns0:note>; refrain thy foot from their path <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">When thou hast any thought, or inclination, or temptation to follow their counsels or examples, suppress it, and restrain thy self as it were by force and violence, as the word implies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 59. 7. Rom. 3. 15.</ns0:note> For their feet run <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">They make hast, as it follows without considering what they are doing.</ns0:note> to evil <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To do evil to others, as was expressed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11, 12. which also will bring evil upon themselves.</ns0:note>, and make hast to shed blood <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To shed innocent blood: which is an inhumane and dangerous practice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Surely in vain the net is spread <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in the eyes of every thing that hath a wing.</ns0:note> in the sight of any bird <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The design of these words is to set forth the folly of these men by the similitude of a Bird, which yet is very variously applied and understood by divers Interpreters. But I shall not confound the Reader with the rehearsal of them. This Clause, <ns0:hi>in vain,</ns0:hi> upon the understanding whereof the whole depends, may be understood, ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. in respect of the Fowler. So the sense is, The Fowler who spreads his Net in the sight of the Bird loseth his labour, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the Bird perceiving the danger, will not be tempted to come to the Bait, but flees away from it. <ns0:hi>But,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>yet, these</ns0:hi> (as the first words of the next Verse may well be, and by the Chaldee Transla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor are rendred) are more foolish than the silly Birds, and though they are not Ignorant of the danger and mischief which these evil courses will bring upon themselves, which I have here represented, yet they will not take warning, but madly rush upon their own ruine. Or, 2. in respect of the Bird. So the sense is, The silly Bird, although it see the spreading of the Net, yet is not at all in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structed and cautioned by it, but through the greediness of the Bait rusheth upon it, and is taken by it. And these men are not one jot wiser, but albeit they know and find that by these practises they expose themselves to the justice of the Magistrate, and to the ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geance of God, the sad effects whereof they daily see in the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction of their Brethren in iniquity, yet they will boldly and madly run themselves into the same miseries. Both ways the sense comes to the same.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. And <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>But,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Yet,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>So,</ns0:hi> for all these ways this Particle is used. Which is more fully expressed in the next Verse. The destruction which they design to others falls upon themselves. <ns0:hi>Their blood</ns0:hi> answers to <ns0:hi>their feet, v.</ns0:hi> 16. & belongs to the san<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e Persons.</ns0:note> they lay wait for their <ns0:hi>own</ns0:hi> blood <ns0:hi>x;</ns0:hi> they lurk privily for their lives.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. So <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">As is expressed both in the foregoing and following words.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the ways <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The actions and courses, which are <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> in the tendency and event of them.</ns0:note> of every one that is greedy of gain <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That seeks gain by unrighteous and wicked practices.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either which greediness: or rather, which gain, by comparing the last words.</ns0:note> taketh away the lives of the owners thereof <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Brings sudden and violent death upon those who had made themselves Masters and Possessors of such gain.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>Wisdom,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>excel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lent Wisdom.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 8. 1.</ns0:note> Wisdom crieth <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Having expressed the counsels and invitations of folly and of wicked men, he now declareth the voice of Wisdom. By the name of Wisdom or <ns0:hi>Wisdoms</ns0:hi> he seems to understand the wisdom for coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel of God revealed to the Sons of men by his Word. Which he calls <ns0:hi>Wisdoms</ns0:hi> here, as also <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 9. 1. either to note the excellency of this Wisdom beyond all other, as the greatest and chief of Beasts is called <ns0:hi>Bebemoth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Beasts,</ns0:hi> Job 40. 15. or because it consisteth of a multitude of wise Precepts, or because it hath been delivered to Mankind at sundry times, and in divers manners, and by ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny Persons, Prophets and Apostles, and especially by the Son of God, who is called <ns0:hi>the Wisdom of God,</ns0:hi> Luke 11. 49. And this wisdom is said to <ns0:hi>cry</ns0:hi> with a loud voice, to intimate both God's earnestness in inviting sinners to repentance, and their inex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cusableness if they do not hear such loud cries.</ns0:note> without <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>abroad,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>in the streets</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>open places,</ns0:hi> as many others render it, and as it is in the next Clause. Not in corners and privily, as Seducers perswade men to error or wickedness, being afraid of the light, but openly and publickly before all the World.</ns0:note> she uttereth her voice in the streets;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. She crieth in the chief place of concourse <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Where there is probability of most success.</ns0:note>, in the opening of the gates <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Where Magi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strates sit in Judgment, and People are assembled. So it crieth both to the wise and to the unwise, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> preached, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1. 14.</ns0:note>: in the city <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Not onely in the gate, but in every part of the City. Or, <ns0:hi>in the Cities,</ns0:hi> the Singular number being put for the Plural.</ns0:note> she uttereth her words, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. How long ye simple ones <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Ye ignorant, and easie, and credulous Persons, who are so soon cheated by the World and the Devil, and do not understand your own Interest.</ns0:note> will ye love simpli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />city <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Being unwilling to part with it or to be made wiser.</ns0:note>? and the scorners <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">That scoff at all Religion, and contemn the Word and faithful Ministers of God.</ns0:note> delight in their scorning, and fools <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Willful and wicked fools, as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 10. & 26. 4.</ns0:note> hate knowledg?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23.
